etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schame, from Old English sċamu, from Proto-Germanic *skamō.

definitions.definition: An uncomfortable or painful feeling due to recognition or consciousness of one's own impropriety or dishonor, or something being exposed that should have been kept private.

quote.citation: 1564 February, Erasmus, “The Saiynges of Aristippus”, in Nicolas Udall [i.e., Nicholas Udall], transl., Apophthegmes, that is to Saie, Prompte, Quicke, Wittie and Sentẽcious Saiynges, […], London:  […]  Ihon Kingston, →OCLC, book I, folio 43, verso, paragraph 42:
quote.text: When he had saied no: what (ſaid Ariſtippus) is it ſhame to ſaile in a Shippe, that hath afoꝛetymes caried a great nomber mo:  […]

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: Have you no modesty, no maiden shame?

quote.text: When this conversation was repeated in detail within the hearing of the young woman in question, and undoubtedly for his benefit, Mr. Trevor threw shame to the winds and scandalized the Misses Brewster then and there by proclaiming his father to have been a country storekeeper.

definitions.definition: Reproach incurred or suffered; dishonour; ignominy; derision.

quote.text: Honour and shame from no condition rise.

quote.citation: 1813, Lord Byron, The Giaour:
quote.text: And every woe a tear can claim  Except an erring sister's shame.

definitions.definition: The cause or reason of shame; that which brings reproach and ignominy.

Waiting for him to leap forward and rip off his flimsy flightsuit, exposing his shame: his illustrated body, Rimmer's cheating frame.

definitions.definition: That which is shameful and private, especially private parts.

definitions.definition: The capacity to be ashamed, inhibiting one from brazen behaviour; due regard for one's own moral conduct and how one is perceived by others; restraint, moderation, decency.

A cry of admonition for the subject of a speech, either to denounce the speaker or to agree with the speaker's denunciation of some person or matter; often used reduplicated, especially in political debates.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English schamen, from Old English sċamian, from Proto-West Germanic *skamēn, from Proto-Germanic *skamāną.

quote.citation: 1692–1717, Robert South, Twelve Sermons Preached upon Several Occasions, volume (please specify |volume=I to VI), London:
quote.text: Were there but one righteous in the world, he would […] shame the world, and not the world him.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cover with reproach or ignominy; to dishonor; to disgrace.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VIII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 13, page 295:
quote.text: And with fowle cowardize his carcas ſhame,

definitions.definition: (transitive) To denounce as having done something shameful; to criticize with the intent or effect of causing a feeling of shame.

quote.citation: 1987 August 15, Mahathir Mohamad, Mahathir Mohamad's letter to Darrell Abercrombie‎[5]:
quote.text: It is disgraceful that you should be used by adults for the purpose of trying to shame us because our extraction of timber from our forests.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To drive or compel by shame.
(obsolete, intransitive) To feel shame, be ashamed.

quote.text: Broder she said I can not telle yow For it was not done by me nor by myn assente  For he is my lord and I am his  and he must be myn husband  therfore my broder I wille that ye wete I shame me not to be with hym  nor to doo hym alle the pleasyr that I can(please add an English translation of this quotation)

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To mock at; to deride.
